subject: Digital Systems and Computer Organization
provenance: Endsem Papers: theory questions adapted from existing Manipal papers, with five newly authored MCQs on selected topics. Worked solutions are AI-authored and computationally checked where applicable.

questions.title: Signed range
questions.markdown:
What is the range of 5-bit two's-complement integers?

**(A)** $-15$ to $15$

**(B)** $-16$ to $15$

**(C)** $-16$ to $16$

**(D)** $0$ to $31$
questions.solution: **Correct option: (B).** For $n$ bits, the range is $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1}-1$, giving $-16$ to $15$.

questions.title: Negative representation
questions.markdown:
What is the 5-bit two's-complement representation of $-9$?

**(A)** `01001`

**(B)** `11001`

**(C)** `10110`

**(D)** `10111`
questions.solution: **Correct option: (D).** Invert `01001` to get `10110`, then add 1 to obtain `10111`.

questions.title: Signed overflow
questions.markdown:
Which addition overflows the 5-bit two's-complement range?

**(A)** $-9+5$

**(B)** $6-13$

**(C)** $11+7$

**(D)** $-4+3$
questions.solution: **Correct option: (C).** $11+7=18$ exceeds the maximum signed value 15; the other results lie in range.

questions.title: PLA arrays
questions.markdown:
Which arrays are programmable in a programmable logic array (PLA)?

**(A)** Both AND and OR

**(B)** Only AND

**(C)** Only OR

**(D)** Neither
questions.solution: **Correct option: (A).** A PLA has programmable AND and OR arrays for constructing and combining product terms.

questions.title: Shared product term
questions.markdown:
A PLA implements $F_1=AB+AC$ and $F_2=AB+BC$. Which product term can be shared?

**(A)** $AC$

**(B)** $AB$

**(C)** $BC$

**(D)** $ABC$
questions.solution: **Correct option: (B).** $AB$ appears in both outputs and can feed both OR connections.

questions.title: POS minimization and NOR implementation
questions.markdown: Simplify $F(A,B,C,D)=\Pi M(0,3,5,6,8,10)$, with don't-care terms $d(2,13,14)$, and implement it using NOR gates only. Take A as the most significant bit.
questions.solution:
Use a K-map with rows AB and columns CD in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10. X denotes a don’t-care.



| AB / CD | 00  | 01  | 11  | 10  |
|:--------|:----|:----|:----|:----|
| 00      | 0   | 1   | 0   | X   |
| 01      | 1   | 0   | 1   | 0   |
| 11      | 1   | X   | 1   | X   |
| 10      | 0   | 1   | 1   | 0   |



Group zeros with useful don’t-cares: $\{0,2,8,10\}$, $\{2,6,10,14\}$, $\{2,3\}$ and $\{5,13\}$. These give
``` math
\boxed{F=(B+D)(\bar C+D)(A+B+\bar C)(\bar B+C+\bar D)}.
```
Each first-level NOR gives the complement of one sum. A final NOR of those four outputs produces their uncomplemented product by De Morgan’s law. Generate $\bar B,\bar C,\bar D$ with tied-input NOR gates: $\bar X=\operatorname{NOR}(X,X)$.



![image](/midsem/figures/nor-source.png)

questions.title: Three-bit magnitude comparator
questions.markdown: Design a 3-bit magnitude comparator for unsigned binary numbers $A=a_2a_1a_0$ and $B=b_2b_1b_0$. Derive the Boolean expressions for $A>B$, $A=B$ and $A<B$, and draw the equivalent logic circuit.
questions.solution:
Define $e_i=a_i\operatorname{XNOR}b_i$. The most significant unequal bit decides the ordering:
``` math
\begin{align*}
G&=a_2\bar b_2+e_2a_1\bar b_1+e_2e_1a_0\bar b_0,\\
E_q&=e_2e_1e_0,\\
L&=\bar a_2b_2+e_2\bar a_1b_1+e_2e_1\bar a_0b_0.
\end{align*}
```
Generate each $e_i$ with an XNOR gate and each complemented input with NOT. The following AND-OR network implements G. Implement L with the same network after exchanging a and b. A three-input AND of the XNOR outputs implements $E_q$. These three networks together form the comparator.



![image](/midsem/figures/comparator3.png)

questions.title: Enabled synchronous up/down counter
questions.markdown: Design a sequential circuit with two JK flip-flops A and B and two inputs E and F. If E = 0, the circuit remains in the same state regardless of the value of F. When E = 1 and F = 1, the circuit goes through the state transitions from 00 to 01, to 10, to 11, back to 00, and repeats. When E = 1 and F = 0, the circuit goes through the state transitions from 00 to 11, to 10, to 01, back to 00, and repeats.
questions.solution:
Let A be the most significant state bit and B the least significant. The state table is:



| Present AB | E=0, either F | E=1,F=1 | E=1,F=0 |
|:-----------|:--------------|:--------|:--------|
| 00         | 00            | 01      | 11      |
| 01         | 01            | 10      | 00      |
| 10         | 10            | 11      | 01      |
| 11         | 11            | 00      | 10      |



A JK flip-flop toggles when $J=K=1$ and holds when $J=K=0$. B toggles whenever enabled. A toggles on an upward carry (B=1,F=1) or downward borrow (B=0,F=0).
``` math
\boxed{J_B=K_B=E},\qquad
\boxed{J_A=K_A=E(BF+\bar B\bar F)}.
```
Equivalently, the second excitation is E AND (B XNOR F). Connect both flip-flops to the same active clock edge and use the following excitation network.



![image](/midsem/figures/jk-updown.png)

questions.title: Three-bit synchronous T counter
questions.markdown: Design a 3-bit synchronous binary up-counter using T flip-flops. Draw the logic diagram.
questions.solution:
For $q_2q_1q_0$, the least significant bit toggles every clock; bit 1 toggles when $q_0=1$; bit 2 toggles when $q_1q_0=11$.
``` math
\boxed{T_0=1,\quad T_1=q_0,\quad T_2=q_1q_0}.
```
All three T flip-flops use the same clock. Feed $q_1,q_0$ through an AND gate to $T_2$. The sequence is $000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111,000$.



![image](/midsem/figures/counter3.png)

questions.title: Four-bit asynchronous ripple counter
questions.markdown: Illustrate a 4-bit asynchronous ripple counter with a neat diagram using JK Flip flops and explain the working of the same.
questions.solution:
Use four falling-edge-triggered JK flip-flops with J=K=1. Apply the external clock to stage 0 and connect each stage’s Q to the next stage’s clock, as shown. Clear all stages to 0 before counting.



![image](/midsem/figures/ripple.png)



The output $q_3q_2q_1q_0$ counts 0000 through 1111 and repeats. Output frequencies are $f/2,f/4,f/8,f/16$. Since changes propagate stage by stage, transitions such as 0111 to 1000 pass through intermediate states. Decoding before the ripple settles can produce glitches. The falling-edge convention is necessary for this Q-to-clock up-counter connection.

questions.title: Byte and word addressing
questions.markdown: Explain the concept of memory addresses in an Instruction Set Architecture. Also, discuss the difference between byte addressing and word addressing.
questions.solution: A memory address identifies an addressable unit of storage. An ISA defines how effective addresses are formed and how load/store instructions interpret them. In byte addressing, consecutive addresses select consecutive bytes. A 32-bit word therefore spans four byte addresses, and consecutive aligned words differ by 4. In word addressing, consecutive addresses select entire words, so consecutive words differ by 1. For $2^a$ addressable units, capacity is $2^a$ bytes in the byte-addressed case and $2^a w$ bytes for w-byte word addressing. Word size and address width are separate concepts.
